key_cases.case_name: Vigil v. Division of Child & Family Services
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the adjudication of domestic violence allegations because DCFS never gave Vigil notice that those allegations would be tried, while affirming the remaining rulings, including the standard of proof applied.
key_cases.relevance: A supported finding that feeds the DCFS Licensing System cannot rest on allegations the subject was never noticed to defend.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the juvenile court erred by adjudicating the domestic violence allegations against Vigil because DCFS failed to provide Vigil proper notice

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the juvenile court's substantiation of the DCFS supported finding that the mother failed to protect her child from a known sex offender, holding the finding was supported by the petition's deemed-admitted allegations and the court's own findings.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Utah model for how a DCFS supported finding is judicially substantiated and reviewed.
key_cases.quote: Because "a foundation for the court's decision exists in the evidence," this court "may not engage in a reweighing of the evidence."

key_cases.case_name: J.J.W. v. State, Division of Child & Family Services
key_cases.holding: The court held that the Juvenile Expungement Statute gives the juvenile court broad authority to order DCFS to expunge its records, including entries in the non-public child abuse Database, but reversed the particular order because DCFS had no notice or opportunity to be heard.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Utah authority for removing a person from the DCFS abuse database, the practical remedy for a wrongful substantiated finding.
key_cases.quote: the plain language of section 78-82-905 grants the juvenile court broad authority to expunge records

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the court of appeals' reversal of a neglect adjudication, holding that nondeferential review was appropriate for the law-like mixed question and that the juvenile court's findings did not satisfy the statutory definition of neglect (or of abuse as an alternative ground).
key_cases.relevance: It shows that an abuse or neglect finding must be tethered to the statutory definition; conduct a court finds troubling is not automatically 'neglect.'
key_cases.quote: the juvenile court's factual findings do not support any of the statutory grounds for neglect

key_cases.holding: The Court held that the court of appeals used the wrong standard when it reversed a juvenile court's finding that an infant was abused and neglected in his father's care, and remanded for review under rule 52(a)'s clearly-erroneous standard, under which findings may be set aside only if they are against the clear weight of the evidence or leave the reviewing court with a firm and definite conviction that a mistake was made.
key_cases.relevance: It governs review of an abuse-and-neglect adjudication, holding that a heightened standard of proof below makes it easier, but never automatic, to show the finding was clearly erroneous.
key_cases.quote: The result must be against the clear weight of the evidence or leave the appellate court with a firm and definite conviction that a mistake has been made.
